planting.note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant after soil has warmed to at least 65°F; seed needs light to germinate and should not be covered.

directions: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; pinch flower spikes regularly to keep the plant productive and bushy through the season. Rama is the classic green-leaved, green-stemmed form of holy basil (tulsi), considered by many Ayurvedic practitioners to be the mildest and sweetest-flavored of the traditional tulsi types, with a fragrant, clove-and-pepper aroma softer than the more pungent purple Krishna form. It is the variety most commonly dried for tulsi tea, prized for its balanced, adaptogenic-reputed flavor, and is also used fresh in Thai and Indian cooking. The vigorous, upright plants produce abundant foliage over a long warm season and, like other tulsi, are considered sacred in Hindu tradition and often grown near the home for both culinary and spiritual purposes. A rewarding, productive warm-season herb for tea and cooking, zone 10–12 or as a warm-season annual elsewhere.

planting.note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant after soil has warmed to at least 65°F; seed needs light to germinate and should not be covered.

directions: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; pinch flower spikes regularly to keep the plant bushy and productive. Krishna is the deep purple-leaved, purple-stemmed form of holy basil (tulsi), named for the Hindu deity traditionally depicted with dark blue-purple skin, and valued both for its striking ornamental coloring and its more intensely spicy, peppery, clove-forward flavor compared to the milder green Rama type. The rich purple foliage and purple-tinged flower spikes make it as much an ornamental accent for a sunny herb bed as a culinary and tea herb, and its stronger flavor makes it a favorite for those who prefer a more assertive tulsi tea. Like other holy basil types, it is considered sacred in Hindu tradition and is easy to grow in a warm, sunny herb garden through the summer. Zone 10–12 or as a warm-season annual elsewhere.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in spring into consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, giving the twining fronds a low trellis, shrub, or fence to climb; only ever use nursery-propagated stock, since wild populations have been historically depleted by over-collection and the species is legally protected in several states.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, with a low support for the twining fronds to climb; never allow the soil to dry out, and avoid disturbing the shallow root system once established. Lygodium palmatum (American climbing fern, or Hartford fern) is a true botanical rarity — the only cold-hardy climbing fern native to North America, found in scattered acidic bogs, moist woodland edges, and stream banks from New England south through the Appalachians. Unlike typical ferns, its fronds do not simply arch from a central crown but instead twine and climb over shrubs and low vegetation, sometimes reaching several feet, giving it a vining habit unique among hardy ferns. Historically over-collected for Victorian-era flower arranging (a practice that led to some of the first plant protection laws in the United States, enacted in Connecticut specifically to protect this species), it remains uncommon in cultivation and should only be sourced as nursery-propagated stock. A genuine botanical curiosity for a consistently moist, acidic, partly shaded woodland garden in zone 5–8.
sources: New England Wild Flower Society — Native Plant Trust

planting.note: Plant tubers or rooted divisions in spring directly into shallow water (2–12 inches deep) or saturated pond-margin soil in full sun to partial shade once water has warmed; duck potato spreads by rhizomes and stoloniferous tubers to form a colony over a season or two.

directions: Plant in shallow standing water or saturated soil at a pond, ditch, or rain garden margin in full sun to partial shade; requires permanently wet to submerged conditions and will not persist in soil that dries out. Sagittaria latifolia (duck potato, broadleaf arrowhead, or wapato) is a native wetland perennial named for its distinctive arrow-shaped leaves rising above the water's surface, and for the starchy, walnut-sized tubers it produces at the tips of its underwater rhizomes — a food source of major historical importance to Indigenous peoples across North America, who harvested the tubers by wading into shallow water and dislodging them with bare feet so they floated free for collection. The tubers have a mild, potato-like flavor and can be boiled, roasted, or fried much like a small potato, while the plant's white, three-petaled summer flowers and bold foliage also make it a valuable ornamental and wildlife plant, providing food for waterfowl (hence 'duck potato') and habitat for aquatic insects. An excellent dual-purpose edible and ornamental for a pond margin or rain garden in zone 4–10.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or plugs in spring directly into shallow water (up to 12 inches deep) or saturated soil at a pond or wetland margin in full sun; softstem bulrush spreads readily by rhizomes to form a dense stand and is often used in constructed wetlands for its strong water-filtering ability.

directions: Plant in shallow standing water or permanently saturated soil in full sun; spreads by rhizomes into a dense colony and tolerates both fresh and brackish water. Schoenoplectus tabernaemontani (softstem bulrush) is a tall, native wetland perennial forming striking, leafless, blue-green, rounded stems that rise straight up from the water like a stand of green pencils, topped in summer with small drooping clusters of brown flower spikelets. It is one of the most widely used native plants for pond margins, rain gardens, and constructed wetlands, valued for its dense root system's exceptional ability to filter and stabilize sediment and take up excess nutrients from runoff, as well as for the cover and nesting habitat it provides for waterfowl, red-winged blackbirds, and other wetland wildlife. The tall, architectural, vertical stems also provide strong textural contrast against broader-leaved pond plants like pickerelweed and arrowhead. An excellent, functional native choice for the wet margins of a pond, rain garden, or bioswale, zone 4–10.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet — Softstem Bulrush
